solution: This is of the form \(\dfrac{0}{0}\). Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate \(\sqrt{6 + x + x^2} + \sqrt{6}\): the numerator becomes \(\left( 6 + x + x^2 \right) - 6 = x(1 + x)\). So the expression is \(\dfrac{x(1 + x)}{x\left( \sqrt{6 + x + x^2} + \sqrt{6} \right)} = \dfrac{1 + x}{\sqrt{6 + x + x^2} + \sqrt{6}}\). Taking \(x \to 0\), this gives \(\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{6}}\). Hence the limit is \(\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{6}}\).

This is of the form \(\dfrac{0}{0}\). Multiply numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{2x + 3} + \sqrt{4x - 3}\): the numerator becomes \((2x + 3) - (4x - 3) = -2(x - 3)\). With \(x^2 - 9 = (x - 3)(x + 3)\), cancelling \(x - 3\) leaves \(\dfrac{-2}{(x + 3)\left( \sqrt{2x + 3} + \sqrt{4x - 3} \right)}\). Taking \(x \to 3\), this gives \(\dfrac{-2}{6(3 + 3)} = -\dfrac{1}{18}\). Hence the limit is \(-\dfrac{1}{18}\).

This is of the form \(\dfrac{0}{0}\). Multiply numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{1 - y^2} + \sqrt{1 + y^2}\): the numerator becomes \(\left( 1 - y^2 \right) - \left( 1 + y^2 \right) = -2y^2\). Cancelling \(y^2\) leaves \(\dfrac{-2}{\sqrt{1 - y^2} + \sqrt{1 + y^2}}\). Taking \(y \to 0\), this gives \(\dfrac{-2}{1 + 1} = -1\). Hence the limit is \(-1\).

Both numerator and denominator vanish at \(x = 2\), so rationalise each. Multiplying above and below by \(\sqrt{2 + x} + \sqrt{6 - x}\) and by \(\sqrt{x} + \sqrt{2}\), the numerator gives \((2 + x) - (6 - x) = 2(x - 2)\) and the denominator gives \(x - 2\). Cancelling \(x - 2\), the expression becomes \(\dfrac{2\left( \sqrt{x} + \sqrt{2} \right)}{\sqrt{2 + x} + \sqrt{6 - x}}\). Taking \(x \to 2\), this gives \(\dfrac{2 \left( 2\sqrt{2} \right)}{2 + 2} = \sqrt{2}\). Hence the limit is \(\sqrt{2}\).

Both numerator and denominator vanish at \(x = a\), so rationalise each. Multiplying above and below by \(\sqrt{a + 2x} + \sqrt{3x}\) and by \(\sqrt{3a + x} + 2\sqrt{x}\), the numerator gives \((a + 2x) - 3x = a - x\) and the denominator gives \((3a + x) - 4x = 3(a - x)\). Cancelling \(a - x\), the expression becomes \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3a + x} + 2\sqrt{x}}{3\left( \sqrt{a + 2x} + \sqrt{3x} \right)}\). Taking \(x \to a\), this gives \(\dfrac{2\sqrt{a} + 2\sqrt{a}}{3\left( 2\sqrt{3a} \right)} = \dfrac{4\sqrt{a}}{6\sqrt{3}\sqrt{a}} = \dfrac{2}{3\sqrt{3}}\). Hence the limit is \(\dfrac{2}{3\sqrt{3}}\).

This is of the form \(\dfrac{0}{0}\). Multiply numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{x + 2} + \sqrt{3x - 2}\): the new denominator is \((x + 2) - (3x - 2) = 4 - 2x = -2(x - 2)\). With \(x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2)\), cancelling \(x - 2\) leaves \(\dfrac{(x + 2)\left( \sqrt{x + 2} + \sqrt{3x - 2} \right)}{-2}\). Taking \(x \to 2\), this gives \(\dfrac{4(2 + 2)}{-2} = -8\). Hence the limit is \(-8\).

This is of the form \(\dfrac{0}{0}\) since \(\sqrt{1 + \sqrt{4}} = \sqrt{3}\). Rationalising once with \(\sqrt{1 + \sqrt{2 + x}} + \sqrt{3}\), the numerator becomes \(\left( 1 + \sqrt{2 + x} \right) - 3 = \sqrt{2 + x} - 2\). Rationalising again with \(\sqrt{2 + x} + 2\), that becomes \(\dfrac{x - 2}{\sqrt{2 + x} + 2}\). Cancelling \(x - 2\), the expression is \(\dfrac{1}{\left( \sqrt{2 + x} + 2 \right)\left( \sqrt{1 + \sqrt{2 + x}} + \sqrt{3} \right)}\), and taking \(x \to 2\) gives \(\dfrac{1}{4 \times 2\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{1}{8\sqrt{3}}\). Hence the limit is \(\dfrac{1}{8\sqrt{3}}\).

This is of the form \(\dfrac{0}{0}\). Multiply numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{a + y} + \sqrt{a}\): the numerator becomes \((a + y) - a = y\). So the expression is \(\dfrac{y}{y\sqrt{a + y}\left( \sqrt{a + y} + \sqrt{a} \right)} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a + y}\left( \sqrt{a + y} + \sqrt{a} \right)}\). Taking \(y \to 0\), this gives \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a}\left( 2\sqrt{a} \right)} = \dfrac{1}{2a}\). Hence the limit is \(\dfrac{1}{2a}\).

Rationalise numerator and denominator separately. The numerator times its conjugate gives \(\left( x^2 + 9 \right) - \left( 2x^2 + 9 \right) = -x^2\), and the denominator times its conjugate gives \(\left( 3x^2 + 4 \right) - \left( 2x^2 + 4 \right) = x^2\). Cancelling \(x^2\), the expression becomes \(\dfrac{-\left( \sqrt{3x^2 + 4} + \sqrt{2x^2 + 4} \right)}{\sqrt{x^2 + 9} + \sqrt{2x^2 + 9}}\). Taking \(x \to 0\), this gives \(\dfrac{-(2 + 2)}{3 + 3} = -\dfrac{2}{3}\). Hence the limit is \(-\dfrac{2}{3}\).

Write \(x\sqrt{x} = x^{3/2}\) and split the numerator as \(\left( x^2 - 1 \right) + \left( x^{3/2} - 1 \right)\), which is legitimate since \(-2 = -1 - 1\). So the limit is \(\lim_{x \to 1} \dfrac{x^2 - 1^2}{x - 1} + \lim_{x \to 1} \dfrac{x^{3/2} - 1^{3/2}}{x - 1}\). Using \(\lim_{x \to a} \dfrac{x^n - a^n}{x - a} = n a^{n-1}\) with \(a = 1\), these are \(2\) and \(\dfrac{3}{2}\). Their sum is \(2 + \dfrac{3}{2} = \dfrac{7}{2}\). Hence the limit is \(\dfrac{7}{2}\).

Rationalise numerator and denominator separately. The numerator times its conjugate gives \(\left( 1 + x^2 \right) - (1 + x) = x^2 - x\), and the denominator times its conjugate gives \(\left( 1 + x^3 \right) - (1 + x) = x^3 - x\). So the expression equals \(\dfrac{x^2 - x}{x^3 - x} \times \dfrac{\sqrt{1 + x^3} + \sqrt{1 + x}}{\sqrt{1 + x^2} + \sqrt{1 + x}}\), and \(\dfrac{x^2 - x}{x^3 - x} = \dfrac{x(x - 1)}{x(x - 1)(x + 1)} = \dfrac{1}{x + 1}\). Taking \(x \to 0\), this is \(1 \times \dfrac{1 + 1}{1 + 1} = 1\). Hence the limit is \(1\).

This is of the form \(\dfrac{0}{0}\). Factorise \(x^2 + x - 20 = (x + 5)(x - 4)\), and rationalise the denominator by multiplying above and below by \(\sqrt{3x + 4} + 4\), which turns it into \((3x + 4) - 16 = 3(x - 4)\). Cancelling \(x - 4\) leaves \(\dfrac{(x + 5)\left( \sqrt{3x + 4} + 4 \right)}{3}\). Taking \(x \to 4\), this gives \(\dfrac{9(4 + 4)}{3} = \dfrac{72}{3} = 24\). Hence the limit is \(24\).

At \(z = 4\) both parts vanish, since \(\sqrt{9} = 3\) and \(\sqrt{1} = 1\). Rationalise each: multiplying above and below by \(3 + \sqrt{5 + z}\) turns the numerator into \(9 - (5 + z) = 4 - z\), and by \(1 + \sqrt{5 - z}\) turns the denominator into \(1 - (5 - z) = z - 4\). So the expression becomes \(\dfrac{(4 - z)\left( 1 + \sqrt{5 - z} \right)}{(z - 4)\left( 3 + \sqrt{5 + z} \right)} = \dfrac{-\left( 1 + \sqrt{5 - z} \right)}{3 + \sqrt{5 + z}}\). Taking \(z \to 4\), this gives \(\dfrac{-(1 + 1)}{3 + 3} = -\dfrac{1}{3}\). Hence the limit is \(-\dfrac{1}{3}\).

Take \(\dfrac{1}{x}\) common: the expression is \(\dfrac{1}{x}\left[ \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{9 - x}} - 1 \right] = \dfrac{3 - \sqrt{9 - x}}{x\sqrt{9 - x}}\). Rationalising with \(3 + \sqrt{9 - x}\), the numerator becomes \(9 - (9 - x) = x\), so the expression is \(\dfrac{x}{x\sqrt{9 - x}\left( 3 + \sqrt{9 - x} \right)} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{9 - x}\left( 3 + \sqrt{9 - x} \right)}\). Taking \(x \to 0\), this gives \(\dfrac{1}{3(3 + 3)} = \dfrac{1}{18}\). Hence the limit is \(\dfrac{1}{18}\).
